intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that autosomal recessive intellectual developmental disorder-43 (MRT43) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the WASHC4 gene (also known as KIAA1033 or SWIP).

checks.evidence_quote: Thus, our findings suggest that SWIP is a novel gene for ARID.
checks.explanation: The abstract supports SWIP as a gene for ARID in one consanguineous family, but it does not mention compound heterozygous mutations and does not explicitly say the change was homozygous.

checks.explanation: The SWIP alias is supported. The alias KIAA1033 does not appear in the abstract.

paragraphs.text: MRT43 is an autosomal recessive intellectual developmental disorder caused by mutation in WASHC4. WASHC4 encodes a subunit of the WASH complex, which takes part in endosomal trafficking. The first family was reported with nonsyndromic intellectual disability (Ropers et al., 2011). Later patients had a more variable, syndromic phenotype that included short stature, macrocephaly or microcephaly, dysmorphic features, skeletal anomalies (Assoum et al., 2020), and skeletal muscle involvement (Gangfuss et al., 2022). Courtland et al. (2021) re-examined the original patients and found that they also had motor symptoms.

paragraphs.text: Assoum et al. (2020) reported 3 patients from 2 unrelated families who had syndromic intellectual disability. Two sisters, aged 4 and 5.5 years, both had learning disabilities, macrocephaly, dysmorphic features, skeletal anomalies, and subependymal heterotopic nodules. The younger sister also had congenital absence of the right internal carotid artery and bilateral sensorineural hearing loss. The third patient, aged 34 years, had mild intellectual disability, short stature, and microcephaly.

paragraphs.text: Courtland et al. (2021) retrospectively re-evaluated the patients reported by Ropers et al. (2011), all of whom were homozygous for the P1019R mutation. Developmental delay or learning difficulties had been the main reason for medical evaluation. However, all of the patients also had motor symptoms (mean age, 10.4 years). Their movements were described as 'clumsy', and clinical examination showed notable fine motor difficulties, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, and mild dysarthria. According to recent communication with the parents, the patients were now an average of 21 years old, and their symptoms had not notably worsened.

paragraphs.text: Ropers et al. (2011) studied a large consanguineous family with autosomal recessive intellectual disability. They combined homozygosity mapping, targeted exon enrichment, and high-throughput sequencing, and after SNP filtering only 2 changes remained. One was a nonsynonymous change in the SWIP gene (WASHC4), which they considered causative because of high pathogenicity and evolutionary conservation scores and functional considerations. The mutation led to significantly reduced SWIP levels and destabilized the entire WASH complex. Courtland et al. (2021) gave this mutation as c.3056C-G, causing a pro1019-to-arg (P1019R) substitution.

paragraphs.text: Courtland et al. (2021) used CRISPR to create mice carrying the human WASHC4 P1019R mutation. In brains of homozygous mutant mice, strumpellin and WASH1 levels were markedly decreased. Spatial proteomics showed that the WASH complex was destabilized, with a decrease in an endosomal module and an increase in a lysosomal module. Cultured mutant neurons had enlarged EEA1-positive endosomes and fewer but larger cathepsin D-positive puncta. In the motor cortex of 7-month-old mutant mice, electron microscopy showed lipofuscin accumulation, and at 10 months, cleaved caspase-3 staining was increased. Mutant mice had persistent deficits in cued fear memory and markedly worse rotarod performance at both adolescence and adulthood. Gait abnormalities appeared by 5.5 months of age, indicating progressive motor decline.

paragraphs.text: Ropers et al. (2011) identified a homozygous nonsynonymous change in the SWIP (WASHC4) gene in affected members of a large consanguineous family with autosomal recessive intellectual disability. The mutation led to significantly reduced SWIP levels and destabilized the WASH complex. Courtland et al. (2021) gave this mutation as c.3056C-G, causing a pro1019-to-arg (P1019R) substitution. They found that it reduced binding of SWIP to strumpellin and WASH1. Mice homozygous for the mutation had markedly reduced WASH complex proteins in the brain, along with cognitive and progressive motor deficits. On re-evaluation, all of the patients homozygous for this mutation had motor symptoms.

agent.process_note: I read all three abstracts (Ropers 2011, Assoum 2020, Gangfuss 2022) in full. For Courtland 2021, I read the Introduction, Results and Discussion in full and skipped the Methods. I searched it for patient, ancestry and consanguinity details. Ropers' abstract does not name the variant or say how many people were affected: the c.3056C>G (P1019R) designation comes from Courtland, and the count of 7 affected individuals comes from Assoum's summary. No ancestry was given for any family. The abstracts give no nucleotide changes for the Assoum variants and do not name the Gangfuss variant, so the Gangfuss variant has no allelic-variant entry. No HGNC reference data were supplied, so I left out the gene's MIM number and chromosomal location.
